# T1 Relaxation

## The two types of signals: Longitudinal recovery (T1)

![The two types of signals: Longitudinal recovery (T1).](images/ch07/the-two-types-of-signals-longitudinal-recovery-t1.png){#fig-ch07-the-two-types-of-signals-longitudinal-recovery-t1}

This chapter and the next describe two of the three basic types of MR signals:  The signals we call *T1* and *T2*.  We will describe how to measure the third type of signal, proton density (*PD*), another time.  This chapter describes the T1 signal.

## The RF signal (B1) causes the net magnetization to precess

![The RF signal (B1) causes the net magnetization to precess: the rotating frame and laboratory frame views (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e).](images/ch07/the-rf-signal-b1-causes-the-net-magnetization-to-p.png){#fig-ch07-the-rf-signal-b1-causes-the-net-magnetization-to-p}

In both cases, for T1 and T2, we begin the measurement process by applying a radiofrequency pulse to the substrate, as we reviewed in the previous chapter. This RF *excitation* is set to a specific temporal frequency, determined by the magnetic field strength, that will cause the *spins* (hydrogen nuclei) to *precess* around the axis of the main magnetic field - the $B_0$ field. That is what is shown in this slide.  The RF pulse causes the net magnetization to tilt over and precess.  Over time, it spins back up to its original state, aligned with the z-axis. Also see @fig-ch06-the-rf-signal-creates-a-precession-signal-of-the-n-1 and @fig-ch06-precession-of-net-magnetization.

## The net magnetization is summarized by two components

![The net magnetization is summarized by two components.](images/ch07/the-net-magnetization-is-summarized-by-two-compone.png){#fig-ch07-the-net-magnetization-is-summarized-by-two-compone}

Conceptually, without any real physical intuition yet, you can see that the net magnetization vector can be separated into two components: one is its projection onto the z-axis, which we call its *longitudinal component*.  The second is its projection onto the x-y plane, which we call its transverse component. 

Because the net magnetization is precessing around the z-axis, its direction in the x-y plane keeps changing.

## The longitudinal component:  High- and low-stability states

![The longitudinal component:  High- and low-stability states (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.6).](images/ch07/the-longitudinal-component-high-and-low-stability.png){#fig-ch07-the-longitudinal-component-high-and-low-stability}

We now start to think about the physical causes for these two components.  It was really a deep insight of the physicists to understand that the source of these two components differs substantially.  Much of the value of the MR instrument arises from the fact that this one signal arises from these different causes.  That is why the MR signal is particularly versatile, and it is something you will want to remember when you think about what you are measuring the the MRI signal.

## Energy from an RF pulse changes spins between the two stable binary states

![Energy from an RF pulse changes spins between the two stable binary states (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.9).](images/ch07/energy-from-an-rf-pulse-changes-spins-between-the.png){#fig-ch07-energy-from-an-rf-pulse-changes-spins-between-the}

The longitudinal signal is described as arising from a difference in the number of spins that are aligned with the main magnetic field (*parallel*), and thus in a relatively low energy state, and the number of spins that are aligned directly opposite (*anti-parallel*) to the main field.  Both of these states are relatively stable, as illustrated in the slide. It shows a bar hanging down in a gravitational field, and that is a fairly stable position.  It is also possible for the bar to be just balanced, completely opposite to the gravitational field.  That is somewhat stable, and it might stay in that position for a while.  But if the bar has any amount of tilt, the gravitational field will pull it down quickly into the low energy, default position. 

## Spin Transition and Quantum Energy

![Spin Transition and Quantum Energy (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.8).](images/ch07/spin-transition-and-quantum-energy.png){#fig-ch07-spin-transition-and-quantum-energy}

To move a spin between two states, we require an RF photon whose energy is matched to the difference in energy between the two states;
 
The energy of an RF photon is $E = hv$ where $h$ is Planck’s constant and $v$ is RF frequency

The RF pulse frequency we need to flip the spins varies with field strength, as explained by Sir Joseph Larmor. For more on Larmor and the relationship between frequency and magnetic field strength, see the resource [Joseph Larmor and his frequency](resources/joseph-larmor.qmd).

The energy in an RF signal at some frequency, $f$, scales with the frequency. The energy - or equivalently frequency - that is required to flips a spin between two states is proportional to field strength, just as the amount of energy to move the bar from the low hanging state to the upright state would depend on the strength of the magnetic field. In the case of electromagnetic theory, we say the energy difference between the two states differs with B0 (*Zeeman effect*).

## The Larmor frequency depends on B0 field

![The Larmor frequency depends on B0 field: $f_L = \gamma B_0$, so the resonant frequency is 127.4 MHz at 3 T.](images/ch07/the-larmor-frequency-depends-on-b0-field-1.png){#fig-ch07-the-larmor-frequency-depends-on-b0-field-1}

The relationship is linear: the Larmor frequency is the gyromagnetic ratio $\gamma$ (42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen) times the field strength.  At 1.5 T we excite and receive near 64 MHz, at 3 T near 127 MHz, and at 7 T near 300 MHz — all in the radio band, which is why the excitation and the receiver are radiofrequency devices.  Higher field strength means a larger energy gap between the two spin states, and so a larger population difference and a larger signal.  That is the main reason for building higher-field scanners.

## Spin-lattice interactions

![Spin-lattice interactions: longitudinal recovery time courses, with T1 of roughly 180 ms for fat, 800 ms for blood, and 2500 ms for free water.](images/ch07/spin-lattice-interactions.png){#fig-ch07-spin-lattice-interactions}

The energy that a spin absorbs from the RF pulse has to go somewhere before the spin can return to its low-energy, parallel state.  It is transferred to the surrounding molecular environment — the *lattice* — which is why T1 is also called *spin-lattice relaxation*.  How quickly that transfer happens depends on the environment, and this is what makes T1 a useful measure of tissue: the T1 time constants in @fig-ch07-spin-lattice-interactions range from a couple of hundred milliseconds for fat to a couple of seconds for free water.

## Example: longitudinal relaxation

![Example: longitudinal relaxation.](images/ch07/example-longitudinal-relaxation.png){#fig-ch07-example-longitudinal-relaxation}

The net magnetization is shown at several points.  The first is the magnetization in the steady B0 field.  Then, an RF pulse at the Larmor frequency is introduced.  This flips the net magnetization away from the z-axis — 90 deg in this example, so that immediately afterwards the longitudinal component is zero.  Then, over time, the longitudinal component recovers toward its steady state value,

$$
M_z(t) = M_0\left(1 - e^{-t/T_1}\right)
$$

Note that this equation is the 90 deg case: it assumes the longitudinal component starts at zero.  The slide asks what would happen with a 180 deg flip angle, which starts the magnetization at $-M_0$ instead.  We take that up in the inversion recovery chapter (@fig-ch10-inversion-recovery-spin-lattice-t1-1), where the negative starting value is the point of the measurement rather than a complication.

## Longitudinal relaxation rate depends on your neighborhood

![Longitudinal relaxation rate depends on your neighborhood: recovery curves for gray matter (T1 = 0.88 s) and white matter (T1 = 0.65 s) at 1.5 T.](images/ch07/longitudinal-relaxation-rate-depends-on-your-neigh.png){#fig-ch07-longitudinal-relaxation-rate-depends-on-your-neigh}

The time course of the net magnetization depends on the material.  So, if we measure the magnetization, say, one second after a pulse, a container with water will have recovered less than a container with lipids.  This difference, which follows from the biochemical structure of the material, is the basis for distinguishing the components of the brain (CSF, gray matter, white matter).

Within the brain the differences are much smaller than the fat/water differences in @fig-ch07-spin-lattice-interactions, but they are large enough to work with.  At 1.5 T the T1 of gray matter is about 0.88 s and of white matter about 0.65 s.  White matter, with the shorter T1, recovers faster and therefore produces the larger signal at any moment during the recovery.

## Contrast: the difference between signals

![Contrast: the difference between signals: the gray/white magnetization difference is largest around 0.8 s after the RF pulse.](images/ch07/contrast-the-difference-between-signals.png){#fig-ch07-contrast-the-difference-between-signals}

What we can actually see in an image is not the signal level but the *difference* between signals — the contrast.  The two recovery curves in @fig-ch07-longitudinal-relaxation-rate-depends-on-your-neigh start together at zero and end together at $M_0$, so the difference between them must be zero at both ends and largest somewhere in between.  @fig-ch07-contrast-the-difference-between-signals plots that difference,

$$
\Delta M = M_0\left(e^{-t/T_{1,G}} - e^{-t/T_{1,W}}\right)
$$

It peaks around 0.8 s after the RF pulse at 1.5 T.  This is a genuinely useful result: it tells us when to read out the signal.  Waiting too long is as bad as not waiting long enough, because both tissues have then fully recovered and there is nothing left to distinguish them.  Choosing the acquisition timing to maximize the contrast of interest is the central design problem of a pulse sequence.

## The T1-contrast distinguishes gray and white matter

![The T1-contrast distinguishes gray and white matter.](images/ch07/the-t1-contrast-distinguishes-gray-and-white-matte.png){#fig-ch07-the-t1-contrast-distinguishes-gray-and-white-matte}

Putting the two ideas together: a longer T1 means a slower recovery, hence a smaller signal at readout, so image intensity runs *inverse* to T1.  White matter (short T1) is bright, gray matter is darker, and CSF (longest T1 of the three) is darkest.  That is the appearance of the coronal, sagittal, and axial images here, and it is why the T1-weighted volume is the standard anatomical image used to separate gray from white matter — for measuring cortical thickness, atrophy, or ventricular enlargement.

The same reasoning, applied to the transverse component, is what produces the opposite contrast in a T2-weighted image (@fig-ch08-t2-weighted-images-white-is-darker-than-gray).

## Surface Interaction Rate (SIR)

![Surface Interaction Rate (SIR); portraits of Bloch and Purcell (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 1.13).](images/ch07/surface-interaction-rate-sir.png){#fig-ch07-surface-interaction-rate-sir}

The T1 of *free* water is a remarkable case.  It can be derived from first principles — Bloembergen, Purcell and Pound worked it out in 1948 (BPP theory) — and the answer, about 4.3 s at room temperature, does not depend on field strength.  Yes, you should be amazed.

Tissue T1 values are much shorter than that (0.65-0.9 s for white and gray matter).  The water in tissue is chemically the same water; what changes is that much of it is near a macromolecular surface.  Interactions at those surfaces speed up the transfer of energy to the lattice, shortening T1.  The T1 we measure in a voxel is therefore a report on how much surface the water in that voxel encounters — which is the idea developed in the next two sections.

## Step 1

![Visualization of the spin-lattice exchange — step 1.](images/ch07/visualization-of-the-spin-lattice-exchange-1.png){#fig-ch07-visualization-of-the-spin-lattice-exchange-1}

## Step 2

![Visualization of the spin-lattice exchange — step 2.](images/ch07/visualization-of-the-spin-lattice-exchange-2.png){#fig-ch07-visualization-of-the-spin-lattice-exchange-2}

:::

So how are we going to use MRI to measure tissue properties?  The build shows a cross-section through a single axon, with the individual wraps of myelin visible, and then a schematic of one layer of the myelin membrane: a lipid bilayer surrounded by water molecules.

The MR properties of water change when it interacts with a membrane surface.  The water immediately in contact with the membrane — the *apparent hydration layer* — has an MR signal distinct from the water further away.  A model based on quantitative T1 mapping can estimate the percentage of the water in a voxel that is interacting with a membrane surface, a measure we call the apparent hydration layer fraction (aHLF).  Because it tracks total membrane surface area, aHLF is much higher in heavily myelinated white matter.

## T1 from multiple molecules:  Fast Exchange Theory

![T1 from multiple molecules:  Fast Exchange Theory (Zimmerman & Brittin, *J. Phys. Chem.*, 1957).](images/ch07/t1-from-multiple-molecules-fast-exchange-theory.png){#fig-ch07-t1-from-multiple-molecules-fast-exchange-theory}

A voxel contains water in several environments at once: water interacting with water, water near a substrate, and water bound to a substrate.  Water in contact with the lattice always has a shorter T1 than free water.

If the water molecules exchange between these environments quickly compared to T1 — the *fast exchange* assumption — the voxel does not show a mixture of separate exponentials.  Instead it shows a single exponential recovery whose *rate* is the concentration-weighted average of the individual rates,

$$
\frac{1}{T_1(L)} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i \frac{1}{T_{1,c_i}} + \left(1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i\right)\frac{1}{T_{1,f}}
$$

Note that it is the *rates* that average, not the time constants.  This is the same bookkeeping that appears in the next chapter, where the rates of two de-phasing mechanisms add to give T2*.  Fast exchange is what makes a single measured T1 interpretable as a property of tissue composition, and it is the basis of the quantitative T1 methods used later in the book.
